spec.title: Inari Paths
spec.subtitle: Vermilion gates, ancient vows, and foxes at the mountain's edge.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · GATEWAY
chapters.heading: Vermilion arches climb the hillside.
chapters.body: Fushimi Inari-taisha is the head shrine of the kami Inari in Kyoto. It sits at the base of Mount Inari, 233 metres above sea level. Trails wind 4 kilometres up the slope, taking about 2 hours to walk. Roughly 10,000 torii were donated by businesses, and about 800 create the Senbon Torii tunnel.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · FOUNDATION
chapters.heading: A clan's arrow birthed a shrine.
chapters.body: The shrine was formally founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, an immigrant group from the Korean Peninsula. Legend says Hata no Irogu shot an arrow at a mochi, which turned into a white bird that landed on Mount Inari. Rice grew where the bird fell, and the deity was enshrined there. The mountain and shrine share the name Inari.

heroImage.attribution: Paul Vlaar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · PURPOSE
chapters.heading: Foxes guard the grain and trade.
chapters.body: Inari is the kami of rice and agriculture, while merchants also honor it as patron of business. Foxes, regarded as messengers, often appear with keys for the rice granary. The shrine hosts as many as 32,000 sub-shrines across Japan. Its main hall offers an open view of a mirror, and the site remains open 24 hours, illuminated at night.
